implementation_notes: In modern .NET the container is the factory: Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection registers each implementation under a service key (AddKeyedScoped/AddKeyedTransient/AddKeyedSingleton) and hands the right instance to a constructor or resolves it on demand, so the factory class disappears entirely. The caller depends on the interface and on a key, never on a concrete class; reach for an explicit factory class again when selection needs logging, validation, fallbacks or per-call parameters that the registration line cannot express.
pitfalls: Keys are strings/objects resolved at run time: a wrong key fails when the service is resolved, not at compile time - prefer constants or enums over literals.
Lifetimes are inherited by whatever the factory captures: resolving a scoped dependency from a singleton factory (or capturing IServiceProvider) creates captive dependencies that live too long.
Registering and resolving through the container per call costs more than direct construction; use ActivatorUtilities only when the implementation type is not known at registration time.

variants.name: Registered Func<TKey, TProduct> resolver
variants.implementation_notes: Before keyed services (and whenever selection needs logic), the everyday C# factory is a registered delegate: AddScoped/Func<string, IPaymentProcessor> holds a switch or dictionary over the concrete types and the consumer takes that delegate as a constructor dependency. It keeps the decision testable (substitute the delegate) without a factory class, and the switch can log, validate or fall back.
pitfalls: Microsoft DI resolves Func<T> only because you registered it; unlike Autofac it will not build a delegate for an arbitrary registered service, so the registration above is mandatory.
A delegate factory captured by a singleton pulls in whatever it closes over: capture IServiceProvider, not a scoped instance.
Callers that resolve fresh instances per call must dispose them; the container disposes only what it created, and only at the end of the scope that created it.

variants.name: Classic abstract Creator with an overridden CreateXxx
variants.idiom_name: abstract class with protected abstract CreateXxx()
variants.implementation_notes: The published GoF form: an abstract base declares the creation operation, subclasses override it, and the base class uses the product in its own algorithm. In C# it is still the right shape when the creator itself is the extension point (a framework base class or template rendered per platform) and the creator has real behaviour beyond creating.
pitfalls: Do not call the abstract CreateXxx from the base constructor: the derived override is not available yet, so initialization must be lazy.
Sealed subclasses plus nullable reference types make the return non-null by contract; keep the signature non-nullable instead of returning null for 'no product'.
